15061(b)(3) (the "Common Sense Exemption"). Moreover, none of the exceptions to the
categorical exemptions contained in CEQA Guidelines § 15300.2 are applicable to the Project.
CEQA Guidelines § 15301 exempts

  "the operation, repair, maintenance, permitting, leasing, licensing, or minor alteration
  of existing public or private structure, facilities, mechanical equipment, or
  topographical features, involving negligible or no expansion of use beyond that
  existing at the time of the lead agency's determination."

Here, the City Council is contemplating the award of franchises for solid waste collection,
transportation, and recycling services. The franchises with the existing solid waste service
providers expire on August 31, 2024. MPMC Chapter 6.09 (approved by voters through Measure
BB) generally requires that the City use a competitive bidding process to choose solid waste
service franchisees not later than August 31, 2024. Pursuant to the MPMC, an exclusive franchise
will be awarded for residential accounts and up to three franchises may be awarded for
commercial accounts.

The services provided pursuant to the Project would be identical to, or substantially the same as,
that currently being provided throughout the City. Therefore, the decision to
approve the Project involves the operation and use of existing facilities and equipment; it does
not involve an expansion of use. Consequently, the Project is exempt from additional
environmental review pursuant to CEQA Guidelines § 15301.

CEQA Guidelines § 15061(b)(3) also exempts the Project from additional environmental
review. That Section provides that

  "[w]here it can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility that the activity in
  question may have a significant effect on the environment, the activity is not subject to
  CEQA."

Here, the Project will not have a significant impact on the environment because the future services
will be identical to, or substantially the same as, the solid waste collection, transportation and
recycling services currently being provided. As is the case with the current service provider,
Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) powered trash collection vehicles will be utilized. Therefore, no
increases in air pollutants or GHG emissions over the baseline conditions are expected. Vehicle
routing will be the same or substantially similar to that currently utilized and the City will retain the
power to approve all routes before the franchise periods begin. This will allow the City to ensure
that arterial streets and intersections with Level of Service (LOS) issues can be avoided during
peak hours.

Solid waste collection – now and in the future – may not commence before 7:00 a.m. or continue
after 6:00 p.m. Solid waste franchisees must comply with MPMC Chapter 9.53 which regulates
noise. All vehicles will be subject to annual noise level testing and certification by the City.

BACKGROUND:
Monterey Park Municipal Code Chapter 6.09, entitled “Solid Waste Franchises,” was
approved by voters on March 8, 2011 by adopting Measure BB. That Chapter requires
the City Council to utilize a competitive bidding process for awarding solid waste
franchises and limits the term of these franchises to seven years. MPMC § 6.09.070
states that

  "[t]he City Council must award the residential solid waste franchise to a
  single franchisee but may, at its discretion, award the commercial solid
  waste franchise to up to three franchisees."

That Section also states that

  "[t]he City Council must award any franchise based upon the applicant
  proposing the lowest proposed monthly rates to the customer. Such rates
  cannot be increased on an annual basis by percentage greater than the
  percentage increase in the consumer price index (“CPl”)….”

The current franchise agreements for both residential and commercial solid waste
collection and recycling services expire on August 31, 2024. Athens Services is the
current residential hauler that provides a two-cart collection system. The current non-
exclusive commercial franchisees are Athens Services and Ware Disposal.

On October 18, 2023, City Council authorized the release of a Request for Qualification
(RFQ) to companies interested in applying for either a residential or commercial franchise
for waste collection and recycling services or both. Ten companies responded to the RFQ

APPLICATIONS RECEIVED:

Residential Franchise:

The City received two applications: Athens Services and Ware Disposal. Athens
residential proposal included both the Two-Cart Collection and Three-Cart Collection
System options, while Ware Disposal only proposed a Three-Cart System option for
residential collection services.

Two- or Three-Cart Collection Systems:

Proposers for residential collection services can bid on two options:

  Option 1 Two-Cart Collection System
  Cart #1 - mixed waste (solid waste and recyclables)
  Cart #2 - organic materials

  Option 2 Three-Cart Collection System
  Cart #1 - solid waste only
  Cart #2 - recyclable materials
  Cart #3 - organic materials

Multi-family residential bin service is the same for Option 1 and Option 2. Recyclable
materials can be collected from source separated bins or carts, or co-collected with the
mixed waste.

Monterey Park residents have been serviced with a two-cart program for over 20 years.
Two-cart systems require the hauler to have access to facilities that can process mixed-
waste to recover recyclable materials. These facilities utilize equipment and conveyor
systems to process waste streams to separate recyclables from solid waste. Facilities
that are designed to only accept pre-separated (i.e., source separated) by the resident
will require a three-cart system (to separate waste from recyclables and organics).

There is ongoing debate within the solid waste industry on the merits of each type of
system. Many companies operating residential source-separation recycling programs
experience contamination problems due to residents placing regular waste in their
recycling carts. This contamination creates operational and financial difficulties for facility
operators since their facilities are not designed to process mixed materials.

Three-cart systems typically have higher collection costs while two-cart systems typically
have higher waste processing costs. Under SB 1383 requirements, organic material in
the mixed waste stream must be processed at a higher diversion facility that can recover

Non-Exclusive Franchises

The MPMC allows the City Council to award commercial franchises to up to three

adjusted annually by the Consumer Price Index. The franchisees would bill their
customers directly for the services and remit franchise fees to the City.

The new franchisees’ services would begin on September 1, 2024 and end on August 31,
2031. The new agreements cannot be renewed or extended.

Single Exclusive Franchise

The MPMC requires the City Council to award franchises to the applicant that proposes
the lowest monthly rates to the customers. Based on the RFAs submitted, Ware Disposal
proposed the lowest monthly rates for commercial service.

If the City Council decides to award an exclusive franchise to Ware Disposal, they would
be required to develop and submit a transition plan that would describe how it would plan
to launch its services to all commercial businesses. The plan would include distributing
new carts and refurbished bins to all commercial customers. The transition plan would
also include copies of education materials that Ware Disposal would distribute to
customers and its routes and customer lists. Ware Disposal would bill its customers
according to the rates provided in its application plus any franchise fees imposed by the
City. Franchise fees collected by Ware Disposal would be paid to the City each month.

3-D.  ENDING THE EMPLOYMENT EMERGENCY FOR THE CITY OF MONTEREY
  PARK EFFECTIVE DECEMBER 31, 2023

  The City Council authorized an employment emergency order in June 2022 to
  expedite recruitment processes in order to fill around 70 positions that were vacant
  at that time. The U.S. labor market had a large gap between job openings and
  workforce participation in 2022 which created a challenging environment for
  recruitment both nationally and locally. The emergency order authorized the City
  Manager to take all reasonable and practicable actions to accelerate the process
  for recruiting, appointing, and retaining persons as City employees to fill all vacant
  positions, including by (1) suspending parts of the City’s personnel rules that are
  interfering with the City’s ability to secure qualified candidates; (2) temporarily
  appointing qualified persons to positions in accordance with Monterey Park
  Municipal Code (“MPMC”) § 2.28.100; (3) amending titles and classifications of
  various positions to make them more attractive to qualified candidates; and (4)
  commencing a substantial overhaul to the City’s personnel rules.

  Every 60 days, staff reported on recruitment, retention, and promotions under the
  employment emergency order to the City Council. Now in December 2023, the City
  has fewer vacant positions and staff recommends ending the employment
  emergency order effective December 31, 2023.

  Action Taken: The City Council received and filed this report and adopted
  Resolution No. 2023-R96 terminating the employment emergency effective
  December 31, 2023 and authorized the City Manager to take all practical actions
  needed to finalize the recruitment and retention of persons for employment, on
  Consent Calendar.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
After dissolving redevelopment agencies, the California Legislature adopted “Economic
Opportunity” legislation in 2014 which allows use of public funds to promote economic
development (SB 470, Wright 2013). Depending on the type of economic development a
city is seeking to promote, a city may be required to make findings to demonstrate that
the development of the property is likely to create jobs, improve tax revenues, or satisfy a
need for affordable housing. Additionally, cities may acquire, sell, or lease real property
in furtherance of economic development (AB 806, Dodd and Frazier 2015).

The City Council’s 2023-24 Strategic Plan includes a goal of Economic Development
within the City. Utilizing elements of the Economic Opportunity legislation may help
advance this goal.

BACKGROUND
Government Code §§ 52200 to 52203 generally allow cities to expend public monies to
help private enterprise for “economic opportunity.” To be classified as an “economic
opportunity,” an agreement or project must fall under any one of the following categories:

  •  Development agreements and other agreements that create new jobs,
  provided that the city council finds that the agreement will create at least one
  new job for every $35,000 spent;

  •  Development agreements that increase property tax revenues, provided
  that the city council finds that the agreement will increase the total property tax
  resulting from the project “at full implementation” at least 15% when compared
  to the year before acquiring property;

  •  Projects leading to the creation of affordable housing, provided that there

  •  Projects that meet the goals of the “Sustainable Communities and

  •  Transit priority projects.

For these economic opportunities, cities may assist a private enterprise as follows:

  Option 1: Acquire, sell, or lease real property. Real property, however, cannot be
  acquired via eminent domain for an economic opportunity. Moreover, real property
  that was acquired by eminent domain (for purposes other than an economic
  opportunity) cannot be sold or leased for less than fair market value.

  Notice and Hearing Requirements for Real Property:

  Acquisition, sale or lease of real property must be approved by City Council
  resolution after a public hearing. Notice must be published for two
  successive weeks before the public hearing; the City must make a report
  related to real property transaction available for inspection including,
  without limitation, a copy of the proposed agreement; information relating to
  the cost of the agreement to the city; the estimated value of the property
  interest; and an explanation as to why the sale or lease of the property
  would benefit economic development.

  Option 2: Issue loans to owners or tenants for rehabilitating commercial buildings
  or structures.

  Notice and Hearing Requirements for Programs and Agreements for
  Rehabilitation of Commercial Buildings:

  The Government Code allows a city to create programs for loaning funds to
  owners or tenants for the purpose of rehabilitating commercial buildings or
  structures. Such loans must be memorialized in loan agreements.
  Additionally, loans may only be authorized after a public hearing after which
  the city council finds that such “assistance is necessary for the economic
  feasibility of the development and that the assistance cannot be obtained
  on economically feasible terms in the private market.” This is the same
  process for public assistance with developing or rehabilitating industrial or
  manufacturing properties.

  Ø Notice and Hearing Requirements for Development Subsidies of $100,000
  or More

A city may also issue an economic development subsidy, such as a bond, loan, or
incentive. Doing so requires a city to comply with certain notice and hearing requirements
before granting an “economic development subsidy” in the amount of $100,000 or more,
and must provide a report showing the efficacy of the subsidy.

An “economic development subsidy” is defined as:

  “any expenditure of public funds or loss of revenue to a local agency in the amount
  of one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000) or more, for the purpose of stimulating
  economic development within the jurisdiction of a local agency including, without
  limitation, bonds, grants, loans, loan guarantees, enterprise zone or
  empowerment zone incentives,1 fee waivers, land price subsidies, matching
  funds, tax abatements, tax exemptions, and tax credits.”2 3

Before approving an economic development subsidy, a city must provide certain
information in a publicly available written form and on the city website. That information
must remain available during the term of the subsidy. That information includes identifying
information pertaining to entities (aside from sole proprietorships) receiving the subsidy;
a description of the subsidy and its purpose; and the estimated number of tax revenue
and jobs generated by the subsidy. The city also must provide public notice and a hearing
before the subsidy may be granted.

Within the term of the grant of the subsidy, but not later than five years following the grant
of an economic development subsidy, a city must issue a report regarding the subsidy.
That report must be available to the public and posted on the city website. The report
must contain the same information provided when the subsidy was first approved. In
addition, it must include information related to the success of the subsidy, such as tax
revenue and number of jobs created. During that time, the city must also hold a hearing
to consider oral commentary on the report. If a particular economic development subsidy
has a term of ten years or longer, the city must also hold a hearing when the term of the
subsidy concludes.

  On October 18, 2023, the City Council approved the release of a Request for
  Qualifications (RFQ) for residential and commercial waste collection and recycling

  qualified to submit proposals.

  The City received a total of five responses to the RFA, two applications for
  residential services from Athens Services and Ware Disposal and two applications
  for commercial services also from Athens Services and Ware Disposal. The three
  remaining companies withdrew from the process for various reasons. Should City
  Council opt for a three-cart collection system for residential waste collection and
  recycling services, the award of an exclusive residential franchise contract would
  be to Ware Disposal that submitted the lowest bid. However, if City Council
  chooses to continue with a two-cart system for residential services, the award of
  an exclusive residential franchise contract would be to Athens Services.

  Staff is requesting that the City Council award an exclusive franchise residential
  franchise to Ware Disposal for a three-cart system, or to Athens Services for a two-
  car system. Staff is also requesting that the City Council award non-exclusive
  commercial franchises to both Athens Services and Ware Disposal, or an exclusive
  commercial franchise to Ware – the lowest bidder.

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
The proposed actions for awarding solid waste franchises (the "Project") were
reviewed in accordance with the California Environmental Quality Act (Public
Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq., "CEQA") and the CEQA Guidelines (14
California Code of Regulations §§15000, et seq.). The Project is categorically
exempt from CEQA Guidelines § 15301 ("Existing Facilities") and § 15061(b)(3)
(the "Common Sense Exemption"). Moreover, none of the exceptions to the
categorical exemptions contained in CEQA Guidelines § 15300.2 are applicable to
the Project.

CEQA Guidelines § 15301 exempts

  "the operation, repair, maintenance, permitting, leasing, licensing, or
  minor alteration of existing public or private structure, facilities,
  mechanical equipment, or topographical features, involving
  negligible or no expansion of use beyond that existing at the time of
  the lead agency's determination."

Here, the City Council is contemplating the award of franchises for solid waste
collection, transportation, and recycling services. The franchises with the existing
solid waste service providers expire on August 31, 2024. MPMC Chapter 6.09
(approved by voters through Measure BB) generally requires that the City use a
competitive bidding process to choose solid waste service franchisees not later
than August 31, 2024. Pursuant to the MPMC, an exclusive franchise will be
awarded for residential accounts and up to three franchises may be awarded for
commercial accounts.

The services provided pursuant to the Project would be identical to, or substantially
the same as, that currently being provided throughout the City. Therefore, the
decision to approve the Project involves the operation and use of existing facilities
and equipment; it does not involve an expansion of use. Consequently, the Project
is exempt from additional environmental review pursuant to CEQA Guidelines §
15301.

CEQA Guidelines § 15061(b)(3) also exempts the Project from additional
environmental
review. That Section provides that

  "[w]here it can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility that
  the activity in question may have a significant effect on the
  environment, the activity is not subject to CEQA."
   72-74
  March 26, 2024

Here, the Project will not have a significant impact on the environment because
the future services will be identical to, or substantially the same as, the solid waste
collection, transportation and recycling services currently being provided. As is the
case with the current service provider, Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) powered
trash collection vehicles will be utilized. Therefore, no increases in air pollutants or
GHG emissions over the baseline conditions are expected. Vehicle routing will be
the same or substantially similar to that currently utilized and the City will retain the
power to approve all routes before the franchise periods begin. This will allow the
City to ensure that arterial streets and intersections with Level of Service (LOS)
issues can be avoided during peak hours.

Solid waste collection – now and in the future – may not commence before 7:00
a.m. or continue after 6:00 p.m. Solid waste franchisees must comply with MPMC
Chapter 9.53 which regulates noise. All vehicles will be subject to annual noise
level testing and certification by the City.

  the “CEQA Guidelines”). CEQA Guidelines §§ 15060(c)(2), 15061(b)(3), and
  15378 exempt activities that will not result in a direct or reasonably foreseeable
  indirect physical change in the environment, activities where there is possibility that
  it may have a significant effect on the environment, and activities that do not

  possible actions are necessary to protect natural resources and the environment.
  Subsequent actions undertaken to protect the environment will be evaluated
  separately under the CEQA Guidelines. Accordingly, this activity is exempt from
  further review.

5-A.  BUSINESS ATTRACTION PROGRAM

  After dissolving redevelopment agencies, the California Legislature adopted
  “Economic Opportunity” legislation in 2014 which allows use of public funds to
  promote economic development (SB 470, Wright 2013). Depending on the type of
  economic development a city is seeking to promote, a city may be required to make
  findings to demonstrate that the development of the property is likely to create jobs,
  improve tax revenues, or satisfy a need for affordable housing. Additionally, cities
  may acquire, sell, or lease real property in furtherance of economic development
  (AB 806, Dodd and Frazier 2015).

  The City Council’s 2023-24 Strategic Plan includes a goal of Economic
  Development within the City. Utilizing elements of the Economic Opportunity
  legislation may help advance this goal.
